elements.text: A family app for running the week together.
One shared plan for the whole family.
The week’s plan, who’s doing what, and something to look forward to, in one place everyone can see.
Families with kids from about 4 to 18.
Parents set the plan. Kids see their own part, tick things off, and can ask for help, a break or a new day.
The week shouldn’t live in one person’s head.
In most families, one parent remembers everything and asks for everything. We think the work, and the credit for it, should be shared.
Points unlock extras the family agrees on.
A climbing wall trip, a movie night out, an allowance if you choose. Everyday time together is never on the line. Bonded keeps track of money; it doesn’t move it.
Bonded is coming to iPhone and Android.

Not at the trash can. At ‘I didn’t know it was my turn.’
‘Clean your room’ means something different to everyone in the house. ‘Clothes in the basket, bed made, floor clear’ doesn’t.

The fridge, a whiteboard by the door, a shared app. Not one person’s head.

Five minutes: what worked, what didn’t, what changes next week. The agreement should keep up with real life.
‘Clothes in the basket, bed made, floor clear’ is hard to argue with.
Soccer is Tuesday. The dentist moved to Thursday. Nobody else knows either of those things.

One thing at a time, next to you.
Toys into the basket, plate to the sink, shoes by the door. They can own it. You’ll still be standing nearby.
Make the bed, set the table, feed the pet. Expect to remind them for a while. That’s normal.
Load the dishwasher, sort the recycling, make their own school lunch. This is where it stops being only about their own stuff.
Their own laundry. One simple dinner a week. The trash on trash day.

How to split jobs between siblings
Five things that help when they’re different ages.
Ten minutes of matching socks at 5 is a real contribution. So is twenty minutes of dishes at 12.
Rotate the unpopular jobs between kids who can do them.
A 12-year-old and a 9-year-old can swap the trash and the recycling week by week. A 5-year-old gets a smaller job that still counts.
A rotation that fits their ages.
Let them help draw it up.
A split they had a say in is much harder to call unfair. Ask what feels fair to them before you decide.
‘Your sister already did hers’ has never once made anyone faster.
What’s fair at 6 and 10 won’t be fair at 8 and 12. The start of each school year is a good moment to rethink who does what.
Same jobs for everyone, or jobs by age?
Washing vegetables, matching socks, watering plants, carrying silverware to the table.
Sensible parents land on both sides of this.
Kids see the connection long before their first job. Saving up means more when they earned it.
Some jobs just come with living here.
Pay for everything and you might start hearing ‘how much?’ every time you ask for help.
Where a lot of families land.
washing the car, clearing the garage
What’s paid, how much, and which day. Most allowance arguments come from an agreement nobody actually made.
Write down what’s been earned as it happens. Then payday is just handing it over.
Which way does your house do it?
Linked, separate, or somewhere in between.
Allowance: linked to jobs, separate, or a mix?
It doesn’t need to be a speech.
Why approvals have room for a note: kids should hear when they got it right, too.
How the Millers, our demo family, use Bonded.
The week goes in, plus one extra to aim for.
Trash on Tuesday, laundry on Thursday, who’s doing what. Then the family agrees on an optional extra for the weekend: a trip to the climbing wall.
Emma has two things on her list. Leo has three. Nobody needs to ask whose turn it is.
He has a practice test, so he asks to swap trash night instead of quietly skipping it.
Every family job that gets done adds points toward the climbing wall. Everyone can see how close they are.
The ordinary stuff isn’t on the line.
Dinners, walks, a parent’s time: none of it depends on points. The points only unlock the extra.
